en: Oṃ. Salutation to the Brahman that is Tat-Sat.
The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad.
The Peace Chant (Śāntipāṭha):
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Worshipful Ones.
With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you and attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
Oṃ, peace! Peace! Peace!
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with uninjured wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ peace! Peace! Peace!

Having pervaded the worlds with the spreading rays of wisdom from the treatises of the Āgamas—rays that extend over the multitude of both the stationary and the moving—I have enjoyed the most abundant pleasures born of desire, yet illumined by the intellect;

having drunk all specific experiences, the consumer of sweetness sleeps through Māyā while making us enjoy her. I bow to that which is the supreme nectar, the unborn Brahman, the fourth state beyond Māyā, which is beyond calculation. //1//

May that Fourth One protect us—he who is the Self of all, who, having first consumed the grossest objects of experience born of ritual injunctions, and afterwards other subtle ones through the power of his own intelligence by means of his own light;
and who, having again slowly established all these within his own self and abandoned all distinctions, is free from the multitude of qualities. (2)
START MandUp 1:
"Om"—this syllable is all this [universe].
Its detailed exposition, which constitutes a compendium of the essence of the meaning of the Vedāntas, begins with the four chapters starting from "Om—this syllable... and so forth.
For this very reason, it is unnecessary to state the connection, subject matter, and purpose separately;

rather, whatever constitutes the connection, subject matter, and purpose in the Vedānta must be the same here as well. Nevertheless, since one wishes to explain this treatise, they ought to be stated briefly.

In this context, the treatise (*śāstra*), being connected to its subject matter through its function of manifesting the means of attainment which possess a purpose, possesses a specific connection, subject matter, and purpose through a traditional lineage. What, then, is that purpose? It is stated: just as for one afflicted by disease there is health upon the cessation of the disease, so too for the self, whose nature is suffering, there is health upon the subsiding of the manifold world of duality (*dvaita-prapañca*).
The purpose is the state of non-duality (*advaitabhāva*).

Since the phenomenal world of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*) is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), its cessation must occur through knowledge (*vidyā*); thus, this work is commenced for the sake of illuminating the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
"For where there is, as it were, duality... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

14) The establishment of this meaning is derived from such scriptural passages as: “Where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another, one might perceive another” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.31); and “But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he perceive? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

In this regard, first is the chapter on the determination of the syllable *Oṃ*, which is primarily based on scripture (*āgama*) and serves as a means for realizing the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*).

Second is the chapter intended to demonstrate, through reasoning, the falsity of that duality upon whose cessation the realization of non-duality occurs— just as the realization of the true nature of the rope occurs when the conceptualization of a snake and so forth ceases.

Likewise, since the contingency of non-duality (*advaita*) itself being false might arise through reasoning, the third chapter is intended to demonstrate its true nature. Since other non-Vedic doctrines— which stand as opposing positions to the realization of the true nature of non-duality— are mutually contradictory and therefore lack reality, the fourth chapter is for the purpose of refuting them by means of the very arguments used against those doctrines themselves.
Furthermore, how is it said that the determination of the syllable *Oṃ* serves as the means for realizing the reality of the Self? It is stated: "This, namely *Oṃ*," (KaU 1.2.15);
"This is the support" (KaU 1.2.17);
"This indeed, O Satyakāma... (PraU 5).
2) “One should unite oneself with ‘Oṃ’” (Maitrī Upaniṣad 6.3);
“‘Oṃ’ is Brahman” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.8.1);
“The syllable Oṃ alone is all this” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.3).
3) From such scriptural passages as these:

just as the rope and so forth are the locus for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a snake and so forth, so too the non-dual Self (*advayātman*), which exists as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), is the locus for the conceptual construction of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; likewise, the entire proliferation of speech (*vākprapañca*)—the object of the conceptual constructions of the Self as the vital breaths and so forth—is indeed the syllable *oṃ* alone.
And that [Self] is indeed the very nature of the Self, because it denotes that [Self].

Furthermore, every conceptualization of the Self, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth—which are denoted by words that are modifications of the syllable *oṃ*—does not exist apart from its designation.
As it is said: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4).
4) "All this is bound together by this [syllable] with speech as the cord, with names as the bonds"—from such scriptural passages as "for all this is indeed names.
Therefore, it is said:
"The syllable *oṃ* is all this; its detailed exposition is: the past, the present, and the future—all is indeed the *oṃkāra*."
And whatever else transcends the three periods of time, that too is indeed the syllable Oṃ.
"Oṃ"— this syllable is all this.

Whatever collection of objects exists as the denoted, because that is not distinct from its designation, and because the designation is not distinct from the syllable Oṃ, therefore Oṃ alone is all this.
Furthermore, since the Supreme Brahman, which is both the designator and the designated, is understood only through a means, it is the syllable *oṃ* itself.

Regarding this very imperishable syllable, which is of the nature of both the higher and lower Brahman—the word "oṃ"—it should be understood that an "explanatory exposition" (*upavyākhyāna*) is now commenced;

the remainder of the sentence implies that an "explanatory exposition" is a clear and detailed explanation presented because it serves as a means for attaining Brahman and stands in close proximity to Brahman.
That which is delimited by the three times—as past, present, and future—is also said to be the syllable *oṃ* alone, according to the reasoning already stated.

Furthermore, that which is beyond the three times, which is to be understood through its effects, and which is undelimited by time, such as the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and so forth, that too is the syllable *oṃ* alone. //1//
START MandUp 2:

Although the designator (*abhidhāna*) and the designated (*abhidheya*) are one, the instruction was given with emphasis on the designator [in the passage beginning] "This syllable *oṃ* is all this. Now, for the purpose of realizing the identity of the designator and the designated, there is again an instruction with emphasis on the designated.
The meaning is as follows:
since the comprehension of the signified depends upon the signifier, there might arise the suspicion that the status of being the signifier is merely figurative with respect to the signified.

Furthermore, the purpose of realizing their identity is so that one may, through a single effort, simultaneously dissolve both the signifier and the signified and thereby realize Brahman, which is distinct from them.
And so he will say: "The quarters are the measures, and the measures are the quarters" (MāU 8).
Therefore it says: "For all this is Brahman; this Self is Brahman. This very Self is four-footed. (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 2)
For all this is indeed Brahman;
that which was stated as being merely the syllable *oṃ*— all that is Brahman.
And that Brahman, which was previously described in an indirect manner, is now specifically pointed out through direct perception as "This Self is Brahman.
By the word "this," he points it out through a demonstrative gesture as the innermost self, being divided into four quarters, saying "This is the Self.
This very Self, denoted by the syllable *oṃ*, is established as both transcendent and immanent; it possesses four quarters like a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin, and not like a cow.

The word "pāda" (quarter) is derived as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), meaning that the realization of the fourth occurs through the successive dissolution of the three [states] beginning with the universal (*viśva*);
alternatively, the word "pāda" is derived as an object (*karmasādhana*), meaning that the fourth is what is reached (*padyate*). //2//

Regarding how there is a fourfold division, he says: Vaiśvānara, whose sphere is the waking state, who is conscious of external objects, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences gross objects, is the first quarter.

"Jāgaritasthānaḥ" means one whose state is the waking state (*jāgarita-sthāna*). "Bahiṣprajñaḥ" means one whose cognition (*prajñā*) is directed toward the external; that is, his cognition is directed toward objects distinct from his own self. The meaning is that cognition appears, produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), solely with respect to external objects.

Likewise, its seven limbs are described [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2]: “Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is *sutejas* (the brilliantly shining), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (the multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartmātmā* (the one whose path is manifold), the trunk is *bahula* (the abundant), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), and the feet are the earth. Thus, as part of the ritual construction of the Agnihotra, the Āhavanīya fire is said to be his mouth; he who possesses these seven limbs is "seven-limbed" (*saptāṅga*).

Likewise, it has nineteen "mouths": the ten organs of perception and action, the five vital breaths beginning with *prāṇa*, and mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness; these are called "mouths" because they are like mouths, meaning they are the gateways for apprehension.
This distinguished Vaiśvānara, through the aforementioned gateways, consumes gross objects such as sound and so forth; thus, he is the "consumer of the gross" (*sthūlabhuk*).
He is Vaiśvānara because he leads all men in manifold ways;
or alternatively, he is Viśvānara because he is both universal (viśva) and a man (nara);
Vaiśvānara is simply Viśvānara with the possessive suffix added.
Because it is non-different from the Self that consists of all aggregates, this is the first quarter.
It is "first" because the realization of the subsequent quarters is preceded by this one.
How is it that this inner Self—of which it has been stated that it is four-quartered as "This Self is Brahman"—has heaven and the other worlds as its head and other limbs?

This is not a fault, because by means of this Self, the fourfold nature of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), including its presiding deities, is intended to be expressed. And this being so, when the entire phenomenal world is stilled, non-duality (advaita) is established.

"The single Self, residing in all beings, should be seen, and all beings in the Self. In this way, the meaning of the Śruti passage beginning with "He who [sees] all beings" (Īśa Upaniṣad 6) is also summarized.

Otherwise, the individual self (*pratyagātman*) would be perceived as being limited solely to its own body, just as it is viewed by the Sāṃkhyas and others; and if that were the case, the distinction established by the Śruti—that there is non-duality (*advaita*)—would not exist, because there would be no difference from the views of the Sāṃkhyas and others.
Yet, it is accepted that all the Upaniṣads aim to establish the identity of the self with the All.

Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that the statement regarding the seven limbs is made with the intention of showing the unity of this internal, embodied self with the cosmic self (*virāḍātman*), which has the heavenly world and so forth as its limbs.
And because of the observation of indicative marks such as, "Your head would have fallen off" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.2),
the singleness of Virāj is intended as an illustration for Hiraṇyagarbha and the Unmanifest Self (avyākṛtātman).

And this has been stated in the Madhu Brāhmaṇa: “This person who consists of splendor and consists of immortality, who is in this earth, and he who is with reference to the self (adhyātma)” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.1), and so forth.
Deep sleep and the unmanifested state—that [Self] is indeed established as oneness because of its being devoid of distinctions.
And this being so, it will be established that non-duality exists when all duality has subsided. //3//
The second quarter is the Taijasa, whose departure is within, who is conscious of internal objects, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences subtle objects. MandU 4.

The dream state belongs to the Taijasa, whose abode is the dreaming state. The waking cognition— which has various means of perception, which manifests only toward external objects, and which consists merely of the vibration of the mind— deposits a corresponding latent impression (saṃskāra) in the mind.
That mind, thus conditioned and like a painted canvas, independent of external means, being impelled by ignorance, desire, and action, appears as if in the waking state.
And so it has been said: "Having taken a portion from this all-encompassing world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9);
likewise, "In the supreme divine mind, [the individual self] becomes one. (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.7)
2) Having introduced the subject with these words, the *Ātharvaṇa* [Upaniṣad] states: “In this state, this deity experiences majesty in dream” (*Praśna Upaniṣad* 4.5).

Because the mind resides within in relation to the sense organs, that wisdom (*prajñā*) which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the mind belongs to him; thus he is "one whose wisdom is entirely internal" (*atyantah-prajña*).
Because it exists as the subject (*viṣayin*) within the wisdom (*prajñā*) that is devoid of objects and whose nature is pure illumination, it is called *taijasa*.
Since the universe possesses objects, the gross wisdom is that which is to be enjoyed;
here, however, the wisdom consisting of mere latent impressions (*vāsanā-mātra*) is what is enjoyed, and thus the enjoyment is "distinct" (*pravivikta*).
The rest is the same;
the second foot is composed of fire. //4//

The qualification "where [he] has slept" and so forth is for the purpose of specifying deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because [ordinary] sleep— characterized by the non-awakening to reality through the functions of perception and non-perception—

is common to both states. Alternatively, since sleep characterized by the non-awakening to reality is indistinguishable across all three stations, [the text] distinguishes deep sleep from the two preceding ones.
That state where one who is asleep desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream—that is deep sleep (*suṣupta*).

In the state of deep sleep, he has become unified, a mass of pure consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), consisting of bliss, an enjoyer of bliss, with the mind as his gateway; this is the third foot, the Wise One (*prājña*). (MandU 5)
MandUpC_5: In whatever place or at whatever time one is asleep and does not see any dream, nor desires any desire—
for in deep sleep, unlike in the two previous states, there exists neither the perception of dreams characterized by misapprehension nor any desire whatsoever.

This is its state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*); thus it is called "having the state of deep sleep. The mind, which was differentiated into two states and vibrated as the manifold world of duality, has now—without abandoning its form—fallen into non-discrimination and become one with the world of plurality (*saprapañca*), like the day swallowed by nocturnal darkness; therefore, the cognitions (*prajñāna*) that were the vibrations of the mind during dreaming and waking have, as it were, become solidified. Because this state consists of the nature of non-discrimination, it is called "the mass of cognition" (*prajñānaghana*).
Just as at night everything is, as it were, a single mass when differentiated by nocturnal darkness, so too [the self] is a mass of pure consciousness (*prajñānaghana*).
By the word "only" (*eva*), the meaning is that there exists no other category distinct from pure consciousness.

Because of the absence of the suffering of exertion involved in the vibration of the mind’s forms as subject and object, it consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—meaning it is predominantly bliss—not bliss itself.

Just as in the world one who remains free from exertion is said to be "an enjoyer of bliss" (*ānandabhuj*) because he experiences this state which consists of absolute lack of effort— according to the Śruti: "This is his supreme bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32)—
so too, because it serves as a gateway for the consciousness that awakens from dreams and so forth, it is called "the mouth of the mind" (*cetomukha*).

Alternatively, it is called *ceto-mukha* because the mind, characterized by cognition, is its door or opening through which dreams and so forth arrive. It is called *prājña* because it possesses the knowledge of the past and the future, that is, the knowledge of all objects;
for even one who is in deep sleep is called *prājña* by virtue of his previous state.
Alternatively, its unique form is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptimātra*); thus, for the wise one, there is also a consciousness distinguished from the other two.
This wise one is the third foot. //5//
He is the Lord of all, He is the All-knowing, He is the Inner Ruler, He is the Source of all; for from Him come the origin and dissolution of all beings.

For this Lord of All, abiding in His own essential nature, is the ruler of the entire multitude of differentiated beings together with the deities; He is not of a different genus from them, as is the case with others.
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "For the mind, my dear, is bound to breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2).
For this very one is the omniscient, because he is known as the knower of everything in all its various states of differentiation.
This very one is also the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), who, having entered within, is the ruler of all beings.
Therefore, since the world with its distinctions is produced [by him] as previously described, he is the source (*yoni*) of everything.

Since it is thus, he who is the source is indeed that very one from whom the origin and dissolution of all beings proceed. (6) Now begin the Gauḍapāda-kārikās: Mandūkya-kārikā 1.1: "The Self alone is all this; there is no doubt about it. One should know that the entire universe is nothing but the Self."
Regarding this matter as it has been stated, there are these verses:
"The pervasive Viśva is one whose consciousness is directed outward; Taijasa, however, is one whose consciousness is inward;
likewise, Prājña is one whose consciousness is dense. Thus, the one alone is traditionally known in three ways. (MandU 1.1)
Regarding the phrase "one whose cognition is directed outward":

because [the Self] exists in three states in succession, and because there is a reconnection through the memory "I am that," it is established—by the scriptural citations of the analogies of the great fish and so forth—that there is a unity, purity, and non-attachment distinct from the three states; this is the intended meaning. //1//
This verse is intended to demonstrate the experience of the three—Viśva and the others—even while in the waking state:
"Viśva is in the right eye; Taijasa, however, is within the mind."
In space, in the heart, and in the intellect—the wise one is thus established threefold within the body.
The mouth is like the right eye; therein, Viśva—the perceiver of gross objects—is primarily experienced. This is according to the Śruti: "He who is this person in the right eye is indeed named Indha.
Indha is Vaiśvānara, whose quality is radiance.
The Vairāja Self is contained within the sun, and the sole seer is within the eye.
But surely, Hiraṇyagarbha is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), while the one who governs the two eyes and is the seer is another, the master of the body.
Not from itself, because difference is not admitted;
for the Śruti says, "The one God is hidden in all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11),
and "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata."
"Undivided, yet existing as if divided among beings" (Gītā 13.16)— according to this Smṛti [text]. Furthermore,
although there is no distinction among all the sense organs, because a greater sharpness of perception is observed in the right eye, the universe is specifically designated therein.
Having seen a form with the right eye, one who closes the eyes and remembers that very same thing within the mind sees it as if in a dream, manifested in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*).
As it is here, so it is in a dream. Therefore, even the Taijasa, while abiding within the mind, is indeed the Viśva.
And when the activity called recollection ceases within the heart-space, the wise one becomes unified and consists of dense wisdom alone due to the absence of mental activity.
For it is only through seeing and remembering that the mind vibrates; in their absence, there remains an undifferentiated abiding in the heart as the self of prāṇa.
This is according to the Vedic scripture: "For prāṇa indeed gathers all these together" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.3).
The Taijasa is Hiraṇyagarbha because he resides in the mind; for it is said,
"The subtle body is the mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6),
and "This person consists of mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.3.2).
This is known from such scriptural passages as these.
[Objection: But surely the vital breath (prāṇa) is differentiated during deep sleep;
therefore, the organs must consist of that [differentiated breath].

How is it that [the state] is undifferentiated (*avyākṛtatā*)? This is not a fault, because the undifferentiated lacks distinctions of place and time. Although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed differentiated when there is the conceit of being the vital breath, nevertheless, the cessation of the conceit of specific limitations within the body results in the vital breath becoming the undifferentiated; thus, for those who possess limited conceits, the vital breath remains undifferentiated during deep sleep.

Just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) becomes unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) for those who identify with the limited [state] during the dissolution of the vital breaths, so too for those who identify with the vital breath, there is an equal state of unmanifestness upon reaching the state of non-distinction. Furthermore, the nature of being the seed of manifestation and its presiding overseer (*adhyakṣa*) are one and the same in the state of the unmanifest.

Thus, the oneness of those who identify with the limited and their presiding overseers is established; consequently, the previously mentioned qualification, "become a single mass of consciousness" (*ekībhūtaḥ prajñānaghanaḥ*), and so forth, is logically justified.
And because the reason has been stated for that [being the unmanifest], how can the term "prāṇa" apply to the unmanifest? It is because of the Vedic scripture:
"For, my dear, the mind is bound by prāṇa" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2).

But is it not the case that there, in the passage "Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), the Brahman that is Being, which is the subject under discussion, is denoted by the word "prāṇa"? This is not a fault, because Being is admitted to have the nature of a seed.

Even though that Brahman is denoted by the word "prāṇa" there, nevertheless, it does not abandon its nature as the seed from which the individual soul (jīva) is produced; for while it exists, it possesses the status of being denoted by the word "sat" (Being).
Indeed, had Brahman been intended here as being devoid of seed, [the scriptures would have used such expressions as] "not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22;
4.5.15) or "from whence words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).

It would have been stated [in the Upanishads] as "That is indeed other than the known and other than the unknown" (KeU 1.3), according to the Smṛti [of the Gītā]: "It is said to be neither existent nor non-existent" (Gītā 13.12).
Furthermore, if [the soul] were dissolved in Being while being seedless, there would be no possibility of rising again from deep sleep or cosmic dissolution.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the rebirth of those who are liberated, since there would be no distinction regarding the absence of a seed;
and if the seed were absent—that is, if it could be consumed by knowledge—then knowledge itself would be rendered purposeless.

Therefore, it is precisely by virtue of its being accepted as a seed that the designation "living being" (prāṇin) is applied to that which exists, and the designation "cause" is applied to it in all the Śrutis.
For this very reason: "Higher than the Imperishable is the Supreme" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2);
"He is indeed unborn, both within and without" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2);
and "From whence words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).
By such passages as “not this, not this” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12), there is a designation [of the Self] through the removal of its state of being a seed.

That state of being a seed— which belongs to that very same reality denoted by the term *prājña*, which is the fourth (*turiya*) state, and which is devoid of the waking state and so forth arising from connection with the body and other limiting adjuncts— he will describe separately as the ultimate reality.

Since one who has arisen [from sleep] observes the cognition "I did not know anything even in the state of the seed [of deep sleep]," it is experienced as being indeed within the body; thus, it is said to be established in the body in three ways. //2//
For the Viśva always experiences gross objects, the Taijasa experiences subtle objects, and likewise the Prājña experiences bliss; understand thus the threefold nature of experience. (MandUkK 1.3–4)
The gross [state] satisfies the universe, while the subtle [state] satisfies the Taijasa;
likewise, bliss satisfies the Prājña—understand this threefold satisfaction.
The two verses have already been explained. //3-4//
Whatever is proclaimed as the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer within the three abodes—
he who knows both of these is the one who enjoys without being tainted.
In the three abodes—waking and the others—the object of enjoyment, known as the gross, the subtle, and bliss, is one though manifested in three ways.
That which is the enjoyer, known as Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña, is proclaimed to be "I" because of the recognition of oneness and because there is no difference in its nature as the seer.
He who knows both of these, divided manifoldly as the enjoyed and the enjoyer, is not tainted while enjoying.
Because every single object of enjoyment is [simply] an object of enjoyment for the one enjoyer;
for that which is the object of someone does not diminish or increase because of him—just as fire, having burned its own objects such as wood, does not [diminish or increase] in that way. //5//
The firm conclusion is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the source of all existing entities;
it generates everything, as does the mind, and the Person (*puruṣa*) produces the individual rays [of consciousness] separately.

The origin—that is, the production—of all existing entities (satām), which consist of the various states of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña, occurs through their own nature as the illusion of name and form created by ignorance.
And the author will state: “The son of a barren woman is not born either in reality or even through illusion.
For if birth were to belong only to non-existent things, then Brahman—which is beyond empirical transaction—would result in non-existence itself, due to the absence of any means for its apprehension.
And it is observed that things such as the rope-snake, which are produced from the seed of illusion created by ignorance, possess existence in the form of their substrata, such as the rope.
Indeed, rope-snakes, mirages, and the like are never perceived anywhere by anyone as being without a basis.

Just as before the production of the snake in the rope, the snake existed as the very essence of the rope, so too, prior to the production of all entities, they exist as the very essence of the seed of the vital breath (*prāṇabīja*).
Therefore, the Śruti also declares: "Brahman alone is this" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11), and "In the beginning, the Self alone was this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.1).
Prāṇa generates everything; from the Puruṣa whose nature is consciousness, the rays of the mind emerge like rays from the sun—forms of consciousness that are like reflections of the sun in water.

The Puruṣa generates these portions of consciousness—which are manifested in the various bodies of gods, animals, and so forth, according to the distinctions of the *prājña*, *taijasa*, and *viśva* states—as distinct from the state of being an object, yet possessing their own characteristics like sparks of fire; and he generates all other states characterized as living beings (*jīva*), like the sun reflected in water.
As it is said: "As a spider [spins its web]... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7). Thus, the Prāṇa, whose essence is the seed, brings them forth.
This is based on such scriptural passages as: "Just as from a fire tiny sparks fly forth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20). //6//
However, others who contemplate creation consider it to be a manifestation or an emanation; by yet others, creation is conceptualized as being like a dream or an illusion. (MandUkK 1.7)

The meaning is that those who contemplate creation consider the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of the Lord of Expansion to be "creation," but for those who contemplate ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no regard for creation;
this is because of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*): "Indra appears in many forms through his powers of illusion" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.5.19).
For one does not [truly perceive] a magician after he has cast a thread into the sky, mounted it along with his weapons, and passed beyond the range of vision.
For those who see it cut into pieces by battle, fall down, and rise up again, there arises a concern for investigating its true nature through means such as illusion (*māyā*).

In the same way, this expansion of deep sleep, dreaming, and so forth is like a magician spreading out a thread; and the one situated therein—such as the *prājña*, *taijasa*, and others—is like the magician mounted upon that [thread]. Just as the ultimate magician is distinct from both the thread and the one mounted upon it, remaining on the ground, concealed by illusion, and invisible, even so is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*) known as the Fourth (*turīya*).

Therefore, noble seekers of liberation (mumukṣu) pay heed only to the contemplation of that [reality], and not to creation which is devoid of purpose; thus, these conceptual constructions belong only to those who contemplate creation. He says, "having the nature of a dream and illusion," meaning they have the form of a dream and the form of an illusion. //7//
Those who have reached certainty regarding creation hold that the Lord’s creation is by mere will;
those who contemplate time believe that the production of beings arises from time.

Because the Lord possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*), creation—such as jars and other things—is merely His will; it is nothing more than the act of intending and does not exist apart from that intention.
Some maintain that creation arises from time alone. //8//
Some say that creation is for the sake of enjoyment, while others say it is for the sake of sport;
this is simply the nature of the Divine, for what desire can there be for one whose every wish is fulfilled? (MandUpK 1.9)

Others consider creation to be for the sake of enjoyment or for the sake of sport. Regarding these two positions, the refutation is as follows: by resorting to the position that "this is the very nature (svabhāva) of the Lord," [it is said] that for one whose desires are fulfilled, what longing could there be?
Indeed, it is impossible to state any cause for the appearance of a snake and so forth in a rope and the like, other than their own nature as ignorance (avidyā). //9//
The fourth quarter (pāda), which follows in sequence, must now be explained; thus he says, "Not inwardly cognitive," and so forth.

Because it is devoid of any ground for the application of any word, it cannot be denoted by words; therefore, he intends to point out the Fourth (turīya) solely through the negation of specific attributes.
In that case, it is indeed empty;

yet it is not false, because it is impossible for a false conceptual construction (*mithyāvikalpa*) to be without a basis (*nirnimitta*). For conceptual constructions such as those of silver, a snake, a person, or a mirage cannot be imagined to have no real locus (*avastvāspada*), being entirely distinct from mother-of-pearl, a rope, a post, or a desert quagmire.

If that is the case, then because the Fourth (turiya) is the locus of all conceptual constructions such as "vital breath" (prāṇa) and so forth, it would be denotable by words; thus, it could not be made known through negations, just as a jar and the like are [known] through their relation to a container of water and so forth.
[But this is not so], because conceptual constructions such as "vital breath" lack reality, just as silver and the like [lack reality] in mother-of-pearl and similar objects.

For there can be no relation between the existent and the non-existent, because such a relation would lack the status of being a real entity (*vastu*) which serves as the ground for the application of words.
Nor can the Self be an object of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because in its own nature it is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), unlike cows and the like.
Furthermore, it does not possess a genus (*jāti*), because, being non-dual, it lacks both generality and particularity, unlike cows and the like.
Nor does it possess activity, because it is changeless like a cook and the like;
nor does it possess qualities, because it is devoid of qualities like blue and the like.
Therefore, it cannot be designated by means of verbal expression.
If it is argued that [the fourth state] is therefore useless because it is equivalent to a hare's horn and the like, we say no;

for the realization of the fourth as the Self is the cause for the cessation of craving for what is not the Self, just as the realization of mother-of-pearl is the cause for the cessation of craving for silver.
Indeed, when the fourth is realized as the Self, there is no possibility of defects such as ignorance or craving.
And there is no reason for the failure to understand that the fourth state (*turīya*) is the Self, since all the Upaniṣads reach their conclusion by having that as their sole purpose:
"This Self is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), and "That is the Truth, That is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.16).
“Indeed, He is unborn, both within and without” (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2);
“All this is indeed the Self” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2), and so forth.

This very Self, consisting of both the ultimate and non-ultimate realities, has been described as having four quarters. Of that [Self], its non-ultimate form—produced by ignorance and comparable to a snake [superimposed] upon a rope—is said to be characterized by three quarters, standing in the relation of seed and sprout.

Now, by means of the negation of the three previously mentioned states—standing respectively for the snake and so forth—he declares the seed-nature, which is the ultimate reality and stands in the place of the rope, with the words beginning "not inwardly cognitive" (nāntaḥprajñam).
"Not inwardly cognitive, not outwardly cognitive, not cognitive of both, not a mass of cognition, not cognitive, not non-cognitive;

unseen, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without marks, unthinkable, indescribable, the essence of the single self-consciousness, the cessation of the phenomenal world, tranquil, auspicious, non-dual—this they consider the Fourth."
That is the Self; that is to be known.

[Objection: But surely, having proposed that the Self consists of four quarters, once the fourth has been established as distinct from the "inner-cognition" (antaḥprajña) and the others by the description of the first three, the negation beginning with "not inner-cognition" is redundant. [Reply:

No, for just as the true nature of a rope is realized through the negation of superimpositions such as a snake, the Self existing in the three states is intended here to be presented as the Fourth (turīya).
It is just like [the teaching] "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.16).

For if the fourth state (*turīya*) were something else entirely distinct from the Self existing in the three states, then, due to the absence of any means for its realization, the instruction of the scripture would be purposeless, or it would result in the fallacy of nihilism (*śūnyatā*).
Rather, just as a rope is conceptualized as a snake and so forth, the single Self alone within the three states appears as "interiorly conscious" (*antahprajña*) and so on.

When it is thus conceptualized, at the very moment the means of knowledge consisting of the cognition that negates [qualities] such as "inner wisdom" (*prajñatva*) arises, the fruit— characterized by the cessation of the manifold of unrealities within the Self—

is fully accomplished. Therefore, in the realization of the Fourth State (*turīya*), no further means of knowledge or other instrument of proof is to be sought, just as when the fruit of the cessation of the snake in the rope occurs simultaneously with the discrimination between the rope and the snake, no further means for the cognition of the rope is required.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates toward the apprehension of a jar by means other than the removal of darkness, it would have to be said that an act of cutting (*chidi*) operates upon one of the two parts even without the separation of the connection between the parts to be cut. However, when a means of valid cognition is engaged in effecting the distinction between the jar and darkness, it culminates in the result of the cessation of darkness, which is not intended as an object of acquisition.

Just as an act of cutting, which proceeds toward the separation of the connection between parts and terminates in the bifurcation of those parts, has the cognition of the jar as an invariable concomitant but that cognition is not the fruit of the means of knowledge; likewise, for the means of knowledge consisting of the cognition of negation— which proceeds toward the discrimination of such qualities as "internal consciousness" superimposed upon the Self— there is no result other than the cessation of the unwanted internal consciousness and so forth.
The application [of the term] to the fourth state (turīya) is logical;
for at the very moment that internal cognition and so forth cease, the distinctions such as being a knower (pramātṛtva) also cease.
And thus he will say: "When [the Self] is known, duality is not found" (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 1.18).
Because knowledge does not persist for another moment beyond the moment of the cessation of duality,
and because if it were to persist there would be the consequence of an infinite regress and thus no cessation of duality;

therefore, it is established that at the very same time as the operation of the means of valid cognition consisting of the cognition of negation, the useless superimpositions such as "inward consciousness" (*antah-prajña*) and so forth, which have been projected upon the Self, cease.
"Not cognizant within" is the negation of *taijasa*; "not cognizant without" is the negation of *viśva*;
"not cognizant both ways" is the negation of the intermediate state between waking and dreaming;
and "not a mass of cognition" is the negation of the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because that state consists in the non-differentiation of the seed-potential.
"Not wise" is a negation of the capacity to know all objects simultaneously;

"not unwise" is a negation of sentience. But how is it understood that internal wisdom and the rest—which are perceived in the Self—are non-existent due to their negation, like the snake [perceived] in a rope? To this it is said:

Even though there is no difference in the essential nature of the Knower (*jñasvarūpa*), its reality is established because it does not deviate anywhere, whereas other things—like the imagined distinctions of a snake or a stream of water upon a rope—do so due to their mutual deviation.
If it is argued that the Knower deviates in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), we say no;
for deep sleep itself is experienced, and according to the Śruti: "For there is no loss of the knower's knowledge" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30).
For this very reason it is unperceived; because it is unperceived, it is beyond conventional discourse and cannot be grasped by the organs of action.
"Without characteristics and without marks"—this means it is not inferable;
for this very reason, it is inconceivable;
and for this very reason, it is inexpressible by words.
It is to be pursued by means of that non-deviating cognition which, in states such as waking and the rest, recognizes: "This Self is one.

Alternatively, it is that Fourth State (turīya) whose realization has the single cognition of the Self as its essence or valid means of knowledge; thus, the Fourth State is "that which has the single cognition of the Self as its essence," according to the Vedic scripture: "One should meditate [upon Him] as 'the Self' alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).
The negation has been made regarding the attributes of the states such as "inner consciousness" and so forth.
By the phrase "the subsiding of proliferation," the absence of the attributes of states such as waking and so forth is expressed.
For this very reason, it is peaceful (*śānta*), changeless (*avikriya*), auspicious (*śiva*), and because it is non-dual (*advaita*), it is devoid of the conceptual construction of difference.
The fourth is considered the *turīya* (the supreme state) because it differs in nature from the three perceived parts.

As it is said, "That is the Self; that is to be known," the Self is the meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), just as the rope is distinct from the snake, the hole in the ground, and the staff that are perceived [in its place]. Thus: "The unseen seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23);
"For there is no loss of the vision of the seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
That which has been described by such passages as these is to be known; once it is known through the understanding of what has previously occurred, the absence of duality is realized. //7//
START MandUpK 1.10 Here these verses occur:
He is the Lord, the Sovereign, the Imperishable, over the cessation of all sufferings.
The non-duality of all existents is remembered by the gods as the pervasive Fourth (turya).
The fourth self (turīya-ātman) is the sovereign (īśāna) when all sufferings characterized by the states of the wise (prājña), the radiant (taijasa), and the universal (viśva) have ceased.
The explanation of the term "sovereign" is "the lord" (prabhu).
The meaning is that he becomes the master with respect to the cessation of suffering.
Because it is the cause of consciousness, it is the cessation of suffering.
It is "imperishable" (*avyaya*) in the sense that it does not depart from its own nature—that is to say, it does not deviate from it.
Why is this so?

Since non-duality exists because all entities are unreal—like a snake [superimposed] on a rope—this very God, because of his luminosity, is remembered as the fourth (*turīya*), the pervasive one who extends everywhere. //10//

START MandUpK 1.11 The relationship of generality and particularity among Viśva and the others is now examined for the purpose of ascertaining the true nature of the Fourth (turya): "Viśva and Taijasa are both held to be bound by cause and effect."
But the wise one is bound by the cause; those two do not exist in the fourth state.
The state of being an effect is "the effect is being produced"; the state of being a cause is "the cause acts.
Due to the non-apprehension of reality and due to apprehension as it [appears], those two—the Viśva and Taijasa as previously described—are held to be bound by these states of seed and fruit.
The wise one (prājña), however, is bound by the very state of being a seed.
For the mere lack of awakening to reality is the seed that serves as the cause for the state of being the wise one.

Therefore, those two—the states of being the seed and the fruit—do not arise from the non-apprehension of reality; the meaning is that they do not succeed, do not exist, and are not possible in the fourth state (turya), which is characterized by true apprehension. //11//

START MandUpK 1.12 But how is it that for the *prājña* (the deep-sleep state) or the *turīya* (the fourth state), bondage— characterized by non-apprehension of reality (*tattvāgrahaṇa*) or apprehension according to [misconception] (*yathāgrahaṇa*)— is not established as being bound by causes?
Because:
The wise one perceives nothing at all—neither self nor others, neither truth nor even falsehood; that fourth state is ever the seer of all.

The wise one does not perceive any external duality—which is distinct from the Self and produced from the seed of ignorance—nor do the Viśva and Taijasa states. Consequently, he remains bound by *tamas*, which consists in the non-apprehension of reality and serves as the seed for erroneous apprehension. However, the Fourth (*turīya*) is always the seer of all; because there exists nothing other than the Fourth, it is "always" (*sadā*) and "existent" (*sat*). Since it is both "all" (*sarvam*) and the "seer" (*dṛk*), it is the "seer of all" (*sarvadṛk*); therefore, the seed characterized by the non-apprehension of reality does not exist [in the Fourth].
In that regard:

even the apprehension of things otherwise, which arises from that [ignorance], is non-existent precisely because of this [Self's nature]; for while the sun is eternally of the nature of light, neither its opposite—non-luminosity—nor its apprehension in another way is possible.
"For there is no loss of the seer's vision."
This is according to the Śruti [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23].

Alternatively, since the appearance of the perception of all objects existing in all states of being during waking and dreaming is indeed the Fourth State (turīya), it is the eternal seer of everything, as stated in the Śruti: "There is no other seer than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11), and so forth. //12//

The non-apprehension of duality is equal for both the conscious state (prājña) and the fourth state (turya). However, the conscious state is accompanied by the sleep of the seed, which does not exist in the fourth state.
This verse is intended to remove the doubt that might arise regarding the attainment of another state.

How so? Since the non-perception of duality is common [to both], there might be the doubt as to why the state of being bound by causes applies only to the *prājña* and not to the *turya*. This doubt is removed because sleep (*nidrā*) consists in the lack of awakening to reality, which is accompanied by the seed-sleep (*bīja-nidrā*).
That very state is the seed for the production of the awakening to distinctions; it is "seed-sleep" (*bījanidrā*), and the *prājña* is endowed with that.

Because its nature is eternal perception (*sadā-dṛk-svabhāvatva*), sleep characterized by the lack of awakening to reality does not exist in the fourth state (*turīya*); therefore, the intention is that there is no bondage of the cause in that state. //13//
The first two [states] are associated with dreaming and sleep; the *prājña* (the wise one) is without dreaming and sleep.
In the fourth state (*turya*), those who are certain perceive neither sleep nor dream.
Dream is the apprehension of things otherwise, like [the perception of] a snake in a rope;
sleep is said to be darkness characterized by the lack of awakening to reality.
Viśva and Taijasa are joined with these two: dream and sleep.
Therefore, those two are said to be "bound by cause and effect.

But the wise one, being joined with sleep alone that is devoid of dreaming, is said to be "bound by the cause" [alone]. Those who know Brahman and are certain of the fourth state (turīya) do not perceive either of these, because they are contradictory, just as darkness does not exist in the sun.
Therefore, the Fourth is said to be unbound by cause and effect. //14//
START MandUpK 1.15 It is said when one becomes established in the fourth state (turiya): for one who perceives otherwise, it is dreaming; for one who does not know reality, it is deep sleep.
When the error regarding these two has been exhausted, one attains the fourth state.
In both dreaming and waking, for one who perceives reality otherwise—as a snake in a rope—there occurs a dream;
for one who does not know reality, sleep is equal across all three states.
Because of the equality of dreaming and sleep, Viśva and Taijasa constitute a single group.

Furthermore, because the apprehension of things otherwise is predominant, sleep is subordinate; thus, in that state, dream is a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*). In the third state, however, sleep alone—characterized by the non-cognition of reality—is the cognitive distortion.

Therefore, when these two states of cause and effect, characterized respectively by the apprehension of things otherwise and by non-apprehension—constituting the bondage of cause and effect—are exhausted through the awakening to the ultimate reality, the fourth state (*turīya-pada*) [is attained].
He attains it;

the meaning is that, no longer perceiving there [in the waking state] that which possesses both characteristics and has the nature of bondage, he becomes certain regarding the fourth state (turiya). //15//
When the individual soul (*jīva*), sleeping through beginningless illusion (*anādimāyā*), awakens, it then realizes the non-dual (*advaita*) reality— unborn, sleepless, and dreamless. (MandUpK 1.16)

This transmigrating individual soul (jīva), through a dream characterized by Māyā—which has proceeded from beginningless time and possesses two characteristics, namely, the nature of non-awakening to reality in the form of the seed-state and the nature of misapprehension—[conceives]: "This is my father, this is my son, this is my grandson;
this is my field, these are my cattle, I am their master; I am happy, I am miserable, I am decayed by this, and I have been prospered by that"—in such a manner.
While sleeping, one perceives dreams in both [the waking and dreaming] states.

When, by a supremely compassionate Guru who is well-versed in the reality of the meaning of the Vedānta, he is awakened with the words, "You are not thus composed of cause and effect, but you are the Reality (Tattva)," then how is he awakened? [The answer is: "In this [Self], there is no external or internal modification of being such as birth and so forth; therefore, it is unborn (aja), meaning it is devoid of all modifications of being, both external and internal."
Because in this state there exists no sleep—the seed of the darkness of ignorance—which is the cause of birth and so forth, it is "sleepless" (*anidra*).
Indeed, that fourth state (*turīya*) is sleepless; for this very reason, it is "dreamless" (*asvapna*), since the apprehension of things otherwise [than they are] has that [sleep] as its cause.
And because it is sleepless and dreamless, one then awakens to the fourth self (*ātman*), which is unborn and non-dual. //16//
START MandUpK 1.17:

If it is argued that one awakens through the cessation of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), then how can non-duality (*advaita*) be asserted as long as phenomenal expansion has not ceased? [The answer is: If phenomenal expansion were to exist, it would undoubtedly cease.
This duality is mere illusion; from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is non-dual.

If the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were real, it would be like a snake imagined upon a rope; however, because it is merely imagined, it does not exist. If it were truly existent, it would undoubtedly cease [upon realization].
For a snake imagined by a deluded perception on a rope does not continue to exist once it has ceased through discrimination.
It is not that the illusion, once employed by the magician, has ceased to exist upon the removal of the visual obstruction for those who see it;

likewise, this mere illusion called "manifestation" (prapañca)—this duality—is in reality non-dual, like a rope or like the magician himself. Therefore, the intended meaning is that from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), no manifestation whatsoever has ever arisen or ceased to exist.
Now, it may be asked: how is the conceptual construction of "teacher," "teaching," and "disciple" to be ceased? It is said:
"Conceptual construction would cease if it were imagined by someone;
this discourse exists for the sake of instruction, but when [reality] is known, duality does not exist. (MandUk 1.18)

If conceptual construction were imagined by anyone, it would cease; for just as this proliferation is like an illusory snake in a rope, so too is this conceptual differentiation of distinctions such as "disciple" and so forth, which arises from instruction prior to awakening. Without that instruction, there would be no such discourse as "disciple," "teacher," or "teaching."
But when the work of instruction is accomplished and knowledge has arisen—once the reality of the ultimate truth is known—duality no longer exists. //18//
START MandUp 8:
That which was explained as the four-footed Self, with the syllable *oṃ* as its primary denotation—
that very Self is this imperishable syllable *oṃ*.
The quarters are the measures, and the measures are the quarters: namely, the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*.

This very Self, being described with primary emphasis on its designation in relation to the syllable *akṣara*, is "the one beyond the syllable" (*adhyakṣara*). But what, then, is that syllable? He says: it is the syllable *oṃ*.

This very syllable *oṃ*, when divided into its constituent parts, exists with reference to the "excessive" (*adhimātra*) measure; thus it is called "excessive. How so? Those which are the feet of the Self are the measures (*mātrā*) of the *oṃ* syllable.
What are they? They are the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*. (8)
Now, a specific rule is established therein:
Vaiśvānara, who has the waking state as his locus, is the letter *a*, the first *mātrā*, because of its attainment (*āpti*) or because it is the beginning (*ādimattva*).
He who knows this indeed attains all desires and becomes the beginning. (MandU 9)
Vaiśvānara, who has the waking state as his sphere, is the letter *a* of the syllable *oṃ*; this is its first matra.
To the question "By what similarity? he says: "Because of pervasion (*āpti*). Pervasion means that by the letter *a*, all speech is pervaded.
For there is the Vedic revelation: "The syllable 'A' is indeed all speech" (Ai.Ā. 2.3.6).
Likewise, by means of Vaiśvānara, the world [is pervaded], as per the Vedic revelation: "Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head itself is *sutejas*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2), and so forth.

We have also stated the identity between the designator and the designated. Because its beginning exists, it is called "beginning" (*ādimat*); just as the syllable named *a* has a beginning, so too does Vaiśvānara. Therefore, on account of this commonality, Vaiśvānara possesses the nature of the letter *a*.

He states the fruit for one who knows that identity: "He indeed attains all desires and becomes the beginning and the foremost among the great, he who knows thus"—the meaning is that he knows the aforementioned identity. //9//
The Taijasa, whose state is that of dreaming, is the letter *U*, the second *mātrā*; it is so because of its excellence (*utkarṣa*) or because it stands between both.
Indeed, one who knows this increases the continuity of knowledge.
And he becomes equal;
in his family there is no one who does not know Brahman, for whoever knows this thus.
The Taijasa, which exists in the state of dream, is the letter *u* of the syllable *oṃ*, the second *mātrā*.

By what similarity? It is said: because of its excellence (*utkarṣāt*). For the letter *u* is, as it were, superior to the letter *a*; likewise, the Taijasa is superior to the Viśva. Because it is intermediate between the two—between the letters *a* and *ma*—the letter *u* is so; and likewise, the Taijasa is between the Viśva and the Prājña. Therefore, due to the commonality of partaking in both states, [the Taijasa corresponds to the letter *u*].
The fruit of the wise is now described: "He indeed elevates the continuity of knowledge";
the meaning is that he increases the continuity of realized wisdom (*vijñāna*).
Being impartial and equal toward the faction of friends as well as toward the factions of enemies, he becomes one who is not hated even by his adversaries.
In the family of one who knows this, there is no one ignorant of Brahman. //10//
The letter *ma* is the wise one (*prājña*), whose sphere is deep sleep; it is the third measure, so called because of measuring (*mīti*) or because of merging (*apīti*).
Indeed, he who knows this measures all this and becomes the merger (*apīti*). 11. Mandūkya Upaniṣad.
The wise one (*prājña*) who exists in the state of deep sleep is the letter *m* (makāra), the third measure (*mātrā*) of the syllable *oṃ*.

By what similarity is this so? He says: "This is the similarity here: the measured (*mita*) and the unmeasured (*amiti*), as well as the measuring (*māna*), are measured by the wise one during dissolution and origination.

Just as barley grains are measured by a *prastha* through entering and exiting, so too the letters *a* and *o* enter and exit the letter *m* at the conclusion of the *oṃ* and at its subsequent application."
Or [it is so] because of non-dissolution (*apīti*).
*Api* here signifies "becoming one" (*ekībhāva*).
For when the syllable *oṃ* is uttered, the final syllable and the two *a*-sounds become as if they have merged into one.
Likewise, Viśva and Taijasa [are absorbed] in Prājña during the state of deep sleep;
therefore, due to this commonality, there is oneness between Prājña and the two forms (Akāra and Ukāra).
He states the fruit for the knower: "He measures," which means he knows this entire world according to its true nature.
The meaning is that he becomes the self who is the cause of the world through delight (*apīti*).
Here, the mention of the intermediate result is for the purpose of praising the primary means. //11//
START MandUpK 1.19 On this point, there are these verses:
When the intention is to express the "atva" (the state of being *a*) of the universe, the excellence of the primordial commonality (*ādisāmānya*) is [established].
And in the case of the non-apprehension of the measure, there would be only the commonality of attainment.

The meaning is that when the state of the universe being merely the letter *a* is intended to be expressed, then the commonality of being "first" (*āditva*) is seen to be intensified and manifested according to the principle already stated.
The phrase "when there is the intention to express its being *a*" (*atvavivakṣāyām*) is explained by the words "when there is the recognition of it being merely a measure" (*mātrāsaṃpratipattau*).
The meaning is: when the state of the universe being merely the letter *a* is recognized.
And because of the word "ca" (and), it follows that the commonality of attainment itself is what is predominant. //19//
When there is clear knowledge of the fiery element, its excellence is clearly seen;
likewise, when there is no comprehension of the subtle elements (*mātrā*), there would be a state of duality of that same kind.

When there is the intention to express the *ātva* (the state of being *a*) and the *ukāratva* (the state of being *u*) of the *taijasa* [element], an excellence (*utkarṣa*) is clearly seen—meaning it is manifest—and its twofold nature is likewise clearly manifest;
everything is as before. //20//
When the letter *ma* is present, there is the *mānasa* state for the wise man, which is another [form] characterized by intensity;
but when there is no perception of the *mātrās*, there is indeed the commonality of dissolution (*layasāmānya*).
The meaning is that when the suffix *makāra* is present, the two [suffixes] *prājña* and *miti* are superior in the case of the general [category]. //21//
He who, being certain, knows that which is equal and common in the three abodes—
that great sage is worthy of honor by all beings and indeed deserving of their salutation.

He who is certain that what has been stated as equal or common in the three aforementioned places is indeed exactly so, becomes one who knows Brahman, worthy of honor and salutation in the world. //22//
START MandUpK 1.23:
Having established the identity of the parts of the Self with the aforementioned generalities and their measures, and having attained the aforementioned Oṃkāra, he who meditates upon it—
the letter *A* leads him to the Universal (*viśva*), and the letter *U* likewise to the Radiant (*taijasa*).
Furthermore, O wise one, the letter *ma* has no course within the non-existent.
The letter *a* leads to and brings about the universal (*viśva*);
the meaning is that the wise one who takes the letter *a* as his object of focus becomes Vaiśvānara.
Likewise, the letter *ā* [leads to] Taijasa.
Furthermore, the letter *ma* leads the wise;
this is understood from the continued application of the word "leads" (*nayati*).

However, when the letter *ma* has ceased—due to the exhaustion of its seed-state—there is no destination whatsoever for the *oṃkāra* that has become measureless (*amātra*). This is the meaning. //23//
The fourth [quarter], consisting of no measure, is beyond conventional usage, the cessation of phenomenal expansion, auspicious, and non-dual. Thus, the syllable *oṃ* is indeed the Self.
He who knows thus enters into himself by means of the self.

That which has no measure (*amātra*) is the *oṃkāra* without parts; it is the fourth, the *turīya*, the Self alone. Because both speech and mind—consisting of the signifier and the signified—have ceased to function, it is beyond empirical usage. It is the cessation of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), auspicious (*śiva*), and non-dual. Thus, for one who possesses the aforementioned realization, the *oṃkāra* employed with its three measures and three quarters is the Self itself.
One enters [it] by means of one's very own Self.

He who knows his own ultimate Self in this way— the knower of Brahman who perceives the supreme truth— having burnt away the third state of being as a seed, enters into the Self and is not born again, because the fourth state is seedless. For when the distinction between the rope and the snake is realized, the snake that had entered the rope does not rise up again as before for those who possess discernment, due to the latent impressions of the mind.

However, for those of dull or middling intellect who have entered the state of a practitioner, who walk upon the true path, and who are renunciants (saṃnyāsins)—for such individuals, the syllable *oṃ* serves as the support for the realization of Brahman when meditated upon correctly, provided they possess the prescribed general knowledge of its measures (*mātrā*) and parts (*pāda*).
And so it will be stated later: "The stages of life (*āśrama*) are of three kinds" (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 3.16), and so forth. //12//
(Thus ends the commentary on the root mantra of the Māṇḍūkya.
Here follow these verses as before: START MandUpK 1.24 pūrvavad atraite ślokā bhavanti (Thus ends the commentary on the root mantra of the Māṇḍūkya. Here follow these verses as before:
One should know the syllable *oṃ* part by part; the parts are the measures (*mātrā*), without a doubt.
Having known the syllable *oṃ* part by part, one should not think of anything at all. (MandU 1.24)
The meaning is that since the quarters (pādas) are the same as the measures (mātrās) as previously stated, and the measures are the same as the quarters, one should know the syllable Om part by part.
Thus, when the syllable Om is known, one should not think of any further purpose, whether seen or unseen, because one's goal has been accomplished. //24//
One should yoke the mind to the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* is the fearless Brahman. For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, no fear exists anywhere. (MandUkK 1.25)
One should yoke—that is, concentrate—the mind (cetas) upon the Praṇava, which is the nature of the ultimate reality (paramārtha) as explained;
for the Praṇava is Brahman, the fearless.
Indeed, for one who is constantly united with it, no fear exists anywhere, according to the Śruti: "The knower does not fear anything from any quarter" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9). //25//
The syllable *praṇava* is indeed the lower Brahman, and the *praṇava* is also remembered as the higher.
The *praṇava* is without prior, without interior, without exterior, and without posterior; it is imperishable.
The *praṇava* is both the higher and the lower Brahman.
When the measures (*mātrā*) and quarters (*pāda*) have ceased, the supreme Self alone is Brahman; thus, because no prior cause for it exists, it is "without antecedent" (*apūrva*).
Because no internal element of a different nature exists within it, it is "without interval" (*anantara*).
Likewise, because no other external thing exists, he is "without exterior" (abāhya);
because no further effect (kārya) exists beyond him, he is "without posterior" (anapara).
For he is both without exterior and interior; the meaning is that the Unborn is a mass of pure consciousness, like a single block of salt. //26//
The syllable *praṇava* is indeed the beginning of everything, as well as its middle and its end.
Having thus known the *praṇava*, one immediately attains that [Brahman].

The origination, persistence, and dissolution of everything—from its beginning, middle, and end—occur just like an illusory elephant, a rope-snake, a mirage, a dream, and so forth, for the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) such as space that arises. Just as the magician and others [are the basis] for the illusory elephant and so on, so too one should know the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) as the Self, which stands in the place of the magician and others; the meaning is that by knowing this, one attains the state of identity with That very instant. //27//
One should know the Praṇava as the Lord, residing in the heart of all;
having realized the Omkāra as all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve. (MandUkK 1.28)

A wise and intelligent person, knowing the Lord— the Omkara who is all-pervading like space, free from saṃsāra, and residing in the heart which is the locus of the causal condition for the memory of all classes of living beings—
does not grieve,
because the causes of grief are no longer applicable.
"From such scriptural passages as, 'The knower of the Self transcends sorrow' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3). //28//
He by whom the syllable *oṃ* is known— that which is without measure, of infinite measure, the cessation of duality, and auspicious— is a sage and a leader of people. (MandUkK 1.29)

The fourth *oṃkāra* is beyond measure (*amātra*). A "measure" (*mātrā*) is that by which something is measured; it is a limitation. That whose measure is infinite is "infinite-measured" (*anantamātra*).
The meaning is that its extent cannot be delimited in this way.
He is Śiva precisely because of the subsiding of all duality.

He by whom the *oṃkāra* is known as it has been explained is a sage (*muni*) because of his reflection (*manana*) upon the reality of the supreme truth; the meaning is that no other person is so, even if they are learned in the scriptures. //29//
